The '''AE86''' series of the '''Toyota Corolla Levin/Sprinter Trueno''' are small, [[Front-engine, rear-wheel-drive layout|front-engine/rear-wheel-drive]] compact cars within the mostly [[Front-engine, front-wheel-drive layout|front-engine/front-wheel-drive]] [[Toyota Corolla (E80)|fifth generation Corolla (E80)]] range—marketed and manufactured by [[Toyota]] from 1983 to 1987 in [[coupé]] and [[liftback]] configurations. It was the last production Corolla to feature rear-wheel drive.

The cars were light, affordable, easily modifiable, and had a five-speed manual transmission, a [[limited-slip differential]] (optional), MacPherson strut front suspension, near 50/50 front/rear weight balance, and a front-engine/rear-drive layout—at a time when this configuration was waning industry-wide.  In certain areas of the world (and optional in others) it was powered by a high revving (7800 rpm) twin-cam engine.  

Widely popular for [[Production car racing|Showroom Stock]], [[Group A]], and [[Group N]], [[Rallying|Rally]] and Club racing, the cars' inherent qualities also earned the AE86 an early and enduring international prominence in the motorsport discipline of [[Drifting (motorsport)|drifting]]. The AE86 was featured centrally in the popular, long-running Japanese [[manga]] and [[anime]] series titled ''[[Initial D]]'' (1995–2013) as the main character's drift and [[tofu]] delivery car. In 2015, ''[[Road & Track]]'' called the AE86 "a cult icon, inextricably interwoven with the earliest days of drifting."<ref name="r&T">{{cite web
 |title       = Understanding the Allure of the Toyota AE86
 |publisher   = Road & Track Magazine
 |first       = Bob
 |last        = Sorokanich
 |date        = 2015-08-25
 |access-date = 2018-07-21
 |url         = https://www.roadandtrack.com/car-culture/classic-cars/videos/a26482/toyota-ae86-petrolicious/}}</ref>

The AE86 would go on to inspire the [[Toyota 86]] (2012–present),<ref>
{{cite web
 |title       = Toyota Sports Car Heritage {{!}} Toyota 86 Predecessors
 |work        = Arabia MSN Autos
 |url         = http://arabia.msn.com/autos/news/ame/2012/may/15820730/toyota-sports-car-heritage-predecessors.aspx
 |access-date = 2012-06-12
}}{{dead link|date=February 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}
</ref> a [[2+2 (car body style)|2+2]] [[sports car]] jointly developed by [[Toyota]] and [[Subaru]], manufactured by Subaru—and marketed also as the Toyota GT86, Toyota GR86, Toyota FT86, Scion FR-S and Subaru BRZ.

In November 2021, Toyota temporarily restarted the production of a limited number of parts for the AE86, with dealers beginning to take orders for new [[steering knuckle]] arms and rear [[brake calipers]]. Rear axle [[half shaft]]s have also been scheduled for new production. Toyota has also announced that this reboot is temporary, and parts will only be available as long as stocks last.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.thedrive.com/news/42961/toyotas-making-new-parts-for-the-ae86-corolla-again |title=Toyota's Making New Parts for the AE86 Corolla Again |first=James |last=Gilboy |work=The Drive |location=US |date=2021-11-01 |access-date=2021-11-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.topgear.com/car-news/retro/toyota-building-new-parts-old-ae86-corolla |title=Toyota is building new parts for the old AE86 Corolla |first=Vijay |last=Pattni |work=Top Gear |location=UK |date=2021-11-02 |access-date=2021-11-15}}</ref>

==Name==
The nameplate ''Trueno'' derives from the [[Spanish (language)|Spanish]] word for ''thunder'',<ref name=trueno5th/> and ''Levin'' derives from the [[Middle English]] for ''lightning''.<ref name="Levin5th"/> In Japan, the car is known colloquially as “Hachi-Roku” (ハチロク), meaning “Eight-Six” in Japanese, which is also used by AE86 enthusiasts outside Japan.

The chassis code "AE86" is used to describe the 1.6 L RWD model of the E80 Corolla. The "A" represents the engine series that powered the car ([[Toyota A engine]] - 1.6 L 4A engines), "E8" represents the generation (E80 series Corolla) and "6" represents the variation within this generation (depending on the engine, drive layout or suspension choice, AE85 is also RWD model but powered by the smaller 1.5 L 3A-U engine, while AE82 is FWD model powered by the same 1.6 L 4A engines). 

Bracketing a minor external facelift, models marketed between 1983 and 1985 are called "''zenki''" (前期, lit. 'early period'), and those marketed from 1986 to 1987 are called "''kouki''" (後期, lit. 'latter period').<ref name=hr>{{cite web |url=http://www.hachiroku.com.au/2008/04/ae86-specifications-history-trim-differences/ |date= April 24, 2008  |website=Hachiroku.com.au |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120211224252/http://www.hachiroku.com.au/2008/04/ae86-specifications-history-trim-differences/ |archive-date=2012-02-11 |title=AE86: An In-Depth Look at A Legend}}</ref><ref name=driftjapan />

The Japanese market AE86 was only available with a [[naturally aspirated]] [[Toyota A engine#First Generation "Blue Top" (Early Bigport)|4A-GEU]] "blue top" {{convert|1587|cc|L CID|1|abbr=on}} [[inline-four engine]], a [[DOHC]] [[Multi-valve#Four valves|four-valve-per-cylinder]] engine, which was also used in [[Toyota MR2 (W10)|MR2 G Limited (AW11)]], [[Toyota Corona (T140)|Corona GT (AT141)]], [[Toyota Celica (A60)|Celica 1600GT-R (AA63)]] and [[Toyota Carina (A60)|Carina 1600GTR (AA63)]] with a [[compression ratio]] of 9.4:1. It had a maximum gross output of {{convert|130|PS|hp kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|149|Nm|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of [[Torque#Machine torque|torque]] in standard form,<ref name=Levin83>{{cite web|url=https://www.banpei.net/japanese-car-brochures/toyota-corolla-levin-ae86-japanese-brochure|title=1983–1985 Toyota Corolla Levin AE86 Japanese brochure|language=Japanese|publisher=Toyota|website=www.banpei.net}}</ref> The 4A-GEU engines used in the Japanese market AE86 were also equipped with [[Denso]] [[fuel injection|electronic port fuel injection]], [[T-VIS]] variable intake geometry and a [[MAP sensor|manifold absolute pressure]] (MAP) sensor.

In North America, a modified 4A-GEC engine was used to comply with California emissions regulations, which uses a [[Mass flow sensor|mass air flow]] (MAF) sensor. Power was rated (SAE net) at {{convert|112|hp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|97-100|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque, while the lower SOHC 4A-C was rated at {{convert|70-74|hp|PS kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|85-86|lbft|Nm|0|abbr=on}} of torque.<ref name="US84">{{cite web|url=https://www.instagram.com/beigeandbluegarage/p/DDU9gHQxCyf/|title=1984 MY Toyota Corolla Brochure: RWD Section|publisher=Toyota USA|via=Instagram}}</ref><ref name="US86">{{cite web|url=https://www.instagram.com/p/CyIvU_Fu06j/?img_index=9|title=1986 MY Toyota Corolla Brochure|publisher=Toyota USA|via=Instagram}}</ref> These North American specification engines were also available in Australia (4A-C only), Sweden, Switzerland and [[West Germany]] (4A-GEC only, from 1985).<ref name="EUAE86L">{{cite web|url=https://www.amayama.com/en/genuine-catalogs/epc/toyota-europe/corolla/AE86L|title=Spare parts for Toyota Corolla, AE86L|website=www.amayama.com}}</ref> However, these engines claimed higher outputs (DIN) at {{convert|116-120|PS|hp kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|140|Nm|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque for the 4A-GEC and  {{convert|78|PS|hp kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|123|Nm|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque for the 4A-C.<ref name="SWI">{{cite web|url=https://www.ae86.ch/AE86/Original_Kataloge.html|title=Swiss market AE86 brochures|language=German, French, Italian|website=www.ae86.ch}}</ref><ref name="GER2">{{cite web|url=https://www.aeu86.org/ae86-brochures/german-ae86-brochure-toyota-corolla-coupe-gt-1985/|title=German AE86 brochure – Toyota Corolla Coupé GT – 1985|language=German|website=www.ae86.org}}</ref> For the rest of the word, the regular 4A-GE (with a MAP sensor) and 4A engines without a [[catalytic converter]] were offered instead. In Europe and selected general markets (such as Singapore<!--same piston part numbers – 13101-16030-->), the twincam engine has a compression ratio of 10.0:1, and is rated at {{convert|124|PS|hp kW|0|abbr=on}} and {{convert|142|Nm|lbft|0|abbr=on}} of torque (DIN).<ref name="AUT">{{cite web|url=https://www.aeu86.org/ae86-brochures/ae86-brochure-toyota-corolla-coupe-gti-1983-11/|title=Austrian AE86 brochure – Toyota Corolla Coupé GTi – 1983-11|language=German|website=www.ae86.org}}</ref><!--The 4A-powered gen-spec SR is likely rated around 79 PS with a 9.0:1 compression ratio, same as the gen-spec AT151 Corona.-->

The AE86 used ventilated [[disc brake]]s for the twincam model, while the single cam featured a front solid disc and rear [[drum brake]]s. The car was equipped with a [[MacPherson strut]] style [[independent suspension]] at the front and a four-link [[live axle]] with [[coil spring]]s for the rear as well as [[stabilizer bar]]s, front and rear, and an optional [[limited-slip differential|LSD]] (twincam with manual only).<ref name="driftjapan">[http://driftjapan.com/blog/toyota/toyota-corolla-ae86 Drift Japan » Toyota Corolla AE86] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629204350/http://driftjapan.com/blog/toyota/toyota-corolla-ae86/ |date=2007-06-29 }} - AE86 History and Overview</ref> Depending on the market, the AE86 came with a T50 5-speed manual [[gearbox]] and optional A42DL/A44DE 4-speed automatic.

Models equipped with the 4A-GE engine received a {{convert|6.7|in|0|abbr=on}} T-series rear differential, while 3A-U (only offered on the AE85), 4A and 4A-C models received a smaller, weaker, {{convert|6.38|in|0|abbr=on}} S-series rear differential.

One of the staff who was behind the car's engineering work was [[Nobuaki Katayama]], who would later head the company's motorsport department and who would become chief engineer of the [[Lexus IS|Altezza]] project a decade later.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lexus.co.za/lexus-life/article/lexus-is-the-evolution-of-an-icon|title=LEXUS IS: THE EVOLUTION OF AN ICON|date=3 June 2021|publisher =Lexus South Africa}}</ref> He has a photo of an AE86 hung in his office.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=CAR Magazine |title=AE86 |date=April 1999}}</ref>

The Levin and Trueno featured fixed-headlights and [[retractable headlights]] respectively, with both available as hatchback or coupé. The export model name Corolla applies to both variations. The AE86 (along with the lower spec {{convert|1452|cc|L CID|1|abbr=on}} [[Toyota AE85|AE85]] and {{convert|1587|cc|L CID|1|abbr=on}} SR5 and DX versions) was [[rear wheel drive]], built on the rear wheel drive [[Toyota Corolla (E70)|E70 Corolla platform]]<ref name=e70861/><ref name=e70862/> (same wheelbase length, interchangeable parts, etc.), unlike the [[front wheel drive]] [[Toyota Corolla (E80)|E80]] models in the same range. The liftback claimed a [[drag coefficient]] of 0,35 Cd, while the coupé was higher at 0,38 Cd.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.banpei.net/2023/10/03/ae86-trivia-levin-trueno-ae86-drag-coefficients|title=AE86 Trivia: the amazing Levin & Trueno AE86 drag-coefficient|date=3 October 2023|website=www.banpei.net}}</ref>

=== Pre-facelift (Zenki) ===
The Japanese market AE86 underwent minor changes in September 1983, it now featured different door mirrors, additional gold stripes for the Levin GT APEX thermostatic flip-up grille and revised optional 14-inch alloy wheels that were now in light gold with new center caps. A sports package was also introduced as factory option, which includes [[bodykit|aero kit]] and leather-wrapped steering wheel and gear shift knob.<ref name="Opt83">{{cite web|url=https://www.banpei.net/2021/07/09/what-was-the-factory-ae86-sports-package-all-about|title=What was the factory AE86 Sports Package all about?|date=9 July 2021|website=www.banpei.net}}</ref>

=== Facelift (Kouki) ===
Minor bodywork changes were made in May 1985, which resulted in different taillights, new sets of alloy wheels, updated bumpers with wrap-around front indicators, corner and headlight trim lights, interior, and grilles. New paint colors were shuffled around as well. Both the Levin and Trueno now had halogen lamps as standard. The seats on the GTV and GT APEX models were also redesigned. These were the main differences for both AE85/86 Levin and Trueno coupé and liftback models.

In 1986, Toyota marketed a limited-edition model of the AE86 as the "Black Limited" model. It was advertised as a limited-production model with only 400 units, and was based on the Kouki Sprinter Trueno GT APEX 3-door liftback.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.banpei.net/2013/12/14/ae86-trivia-sprinter-trueno-ae86-black-limited-facts |title=AE86 Trivia: all Sprinter Trueno AE86 Black Limited facts |website=Banpei.net |location=The Netherlands |date=2013-12-14 |access-date=2020-06-25}}</ref>

In the early 1987, there was a soft-top convertible version based on the Sprinter Trueno GT APEX coupé sold by a [[Toyota dealerships (Japan)|Toyota Auto Store]] dealer in [[Tama, Tokyo]]. Approximately 20 units of this dealer optional model were produced, priced at almost 50% more than the top model Sprinter Trueno.<ref name="convertible1"/><ref name="convertible2" />

==Models and specifications==

In Japan, the DOHC 4A-GEU AE86 was offered in GT, GTV and GT APEX [[trim package|trims]] as the Corolla Levin or Sprinter Trueno. All AE86 models produced for Japan featured the 1.6 L 4A-GEU engine, while all AE85 models had the smaller 1.5 L 3A-U engine and not available everywhere else.<ref name=Levinzenki/><ref name=Levinkouki>{{cite web|url=https://www.toyota.co.jp/jpn/company/history/75years/vehicle_lineage/catalog/60003763/html5m.html#page=1|title=75 years of Toyota - Corolla Levin 5th brochure (1985–1987)|language=Japanese|publisher=Toyota }}</ref>

=== Japanese model variations ===
{{unreferenced section|date=April 2023}}
==== GT APEX ====
This trim level is the highest level of the AE86, offered in both 2-door and 3-door body styles and coming in both Levin and Trueno versions.

On the exterior, three two-tone paint colors are available, a standard 13-inch alloy wheels and had brown-tinted glass (a feature unique to the GT APEX only, as all other models (including export models) had blue-tinted glass instead). It has power mirrors, adjustable interval windshield wipers, and a rear windshield wiper on liftback models. A special thermostatic flip-up grille was also available as an option on the Levin for the Zenki models. On the interior, they have the interior of the AE86 GT, with a three-spoke steering wheel, sport seats, split-folding rear seat, power steering, a tilting steering column, rear defrost, air conditioning, manual windows, and interior illumination dimming. A five-speed manual transmission is standard, with the option of a four-speed automatic transmission being offered on the Kouki models.

Options for this model include (but not limited to): limited-slip differential (LSD), cruise control, power windows, power sunroof, digital instrument cluster (standard on zenki liftback), automatic air conditioning, OEM aero sports package (available after Sep 1983), optional 14-inch alloy wheels, [[Alpine Electronics|Alpine]] sound system, fog lights on the Levin (Kouki models only), mudflaps, and rear hatch visor and quarter window billboards.

[[File:AE86 GT APEX Electronic Display.jpg|thumb|left|GT APEX optional digital instrument cluster]]

==== GTV ====
This trim level is the upmarket lightweight-sports grade level of the AE86, coming in both Levin and Trueno versions. It was only offered in the 3-door body style. It features the interior of the AE86 GT, with a three-spoke steering wheel, smaller center console, sport seats, split-folding rear seat, illumination dimming, and manual mirrors and windows. It had blue-tinted glass on the exterior, and had 14-inch steel wheels with disk brakes on the front and rear. Side door decals denoting "GTV Twin Cam 16" were added, exclusive to this model. A five-speed manual transmission is standard.

Options include (but not limited to): two-tone paint colors, air conditioning, power steering, power mirrors, power sunroof, rear wipers, limited-slip differential (LSD), optional 14-inch alloy wheels, OEM aero sports package (available after Sep 1983), mudflaps and body-colored bumpers.

==== GT ====
The GT trim level is the base model of the AE86. It was only offered in the 2-door body style and came in both Levin and Trueno versions. It used the interior of the AE85 SE, with a basic two-spoke steering wheel, smaller center console, basic seats, non split-folding rear seat, and manual mirrors and windows. It had blue-tinted glass on the exterior, and had 13-inch steel wheels with basic disk brakes on the front and drum brakes on the rear. A five-speed manual transmission was standard, with the option of a four-speed automatic transmission being offered on the Kouki models.

Options include (but not limited to): air conditioning, power steering, power mirrors, power sunroof, limited-slip differential (LSD), optional 14-inch alloy wheels, OEM aero sports package (available after Sep 1983), mudflaps, automatic transmission (Kouki models only), and rear defrost.

The GT models were the lightest out of any AE86 models, weighing in at about {{Convert|900|kg|lb|0|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Levinzenki/>

===North American AE86 specifications===
{{More citations needed section|date=April 2023|reason=The single reference covers only a minor point}}
The AE86 was sold in North America as the Corolla Sport, but initially only the DX and SR5 with the SOHC 4A-C engine, until the top-spec DOHC 4A-GEC GT-S was added in August 1984.<ref name=AE86USmodels/> The DX was generally an internal Toyota designation, as brochures and advertising do not include the DX designation, hence it was more uncommon than the SR5 and GT-S.

Both body styles were sold with Trueno [[pop-up headlights]] and Levin taillights, a different two-spoke steering wheel, and had longer, heavier 5 mph (8 km/h) regulated bumpers in the front and rear. A minor facelift was occurred in the middle of 1985 (1986 MY), it can be identified by the new taillights, steering wheel and aluminium wheels.

====DX & SR5 specifications====
Lower-spec North American AE86 models such as the Sport SR5 used the {{convert|1587|cc|L|1|abbr=on}} 4A-C [[SOHC]] unit, The S-series rear end was a 6.38-inch non-LSD with [[drum brake]]s. The SR5 model also had a softer suspension, and small styling and interior changes such as seats, gauge cluster, door panels, un-painted matte black front and rear bumpers, the lower part of the front bumper surround is shorter and flat, and its VIN differs as well, being AE86 for the SR5 model (for North American market cars). The Sport SR5 can also be identified by the "X" identification on the 4th digit of the model code, found on the chassis plate.<ref name="gojunen">{{cite book |publisher=Magazine Box | series = M.B. MOOK |title=トヨタ・カローラ50年とその時代 |trans-title=Toyota Corolla's 50 years |location=Japan |language=ja |date=2016-10-31 |isbn=978-4866400150}}</ref>

Another lower-spec AE86 model was the base-model DX coupé (US only), which had the same {{convert|1587|cc|L|1|abbr=on}} 4A-C [[SOHC]] unit and 6.38-inch non-LSD rear end with [[drum brake]]s as the SR5. While being near-identical to the SR5, the DX lacks many of the options and features that were present on the SR5 and GT-S, such as a smaller center console, no rear sway bars, tiny wheels center caps, fuel door with a key hole (84–86), no air conditioning, non split rear bench seat and a very basic interior. The VIN of the DX is AE85 (not to be confused with the Japan-only [[Toyota AE85|AE85]]), but its chassis code on the engine firewall remained as AE86. The base-model DX can also be identified with the "D" identification on the 4th digit of the model code, found on the chassis plate.<ref name="gojunen"/>

===Rest of the world===
The European market AE86 was based on the Corolla Levin and marketed as the Corolla GT (or GTi) and SR, the latter was only offered in Sweden and Switzerland. Unlike the Levin, this model featured a front grille with a "TOYOTA" badge instead of "LEVIN". In the 1985 facelift, only the front end was revised. Both body styles were available in Europe, but depending on the country, not all body styles were offered. For example, the coupé was the only option in the Netherlands, and the liftback was the only option in the UK/Ireland, but both were available in West Germany.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.autoweek.nl/autobrochures/download/662/|title= E80 Corolla Sedan, Liftback, Stationwagon & Coupé GT|language=Dutch}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.curbsideclassic.com/vintage-reviews/1980s-vintage-reviews/asian-brands-1980s-vintage-reviews/vintage-review-1984-toyota-corolla-gt-ae86-uk/|title=Vintage Review: 1984 Toyota Corolla (AE86) GT Coupe – Drift King In The UK|website=www.curbsideclassic.com}}</ref><ref name="EUAE86L"/> Other exterior differences can be identified by the additional turn signal on the front fenders, rear license plate lights that illuminate from below, fuel door with a key hole, standard aero kit, hubcaps (pre-facelift) and optional headlights washer. The interior and equipments are very similar to the kouki JDM GTV and AE85 SR. The 4A-GE engine with a MAP sensor and without a catalytic converter was the only option in Europe, except for Sweden and Switzerland, which were initially only offered the SR liftback with the 4A-C engine.<ref name="EUAE86L"/> In 1985, the North American 4A-GEC became the standard engine in Sweden and Switzerland, but also as an option in West Germany and sold alongside the regular 4A-GE version.<ref name="EUAE86L"/><ref name="GER2"/> The T50 five-speed manual was the only gearbox in Europe, an optional T283 LSD was also available.

The general markets (selected countries in the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Caribbean islands) AE86 was also sold as GT and SR. The former was a liftback, while the latter was available for both body styles. It is very identical to the European model, but lacked the additional turn signal on the front fenders and headlight washer, but featured a standard internal fuel door opener.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.instagram.com/p/Cq1mjA_Sm-n/?img_index=1|title=New Zealand new AE86 GT liftback at Toyota fest|via=Instagram}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.facebook.com/groups/704449719694132/posts/3048900761915671/|title=Chilean market AE86 Corolla GT liftback|language=Spanish|via=Facebook}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E2i2hHr7bsg|title=AE86 SR coupé in Jordan|language=Arabic|via=YouTube}}</ref> The GT was only paired to a five-speed manual and also with an optional LSD, while four-speed automatic was available as an option for the SOHC 4A-powered SR.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amayama.com/en/genuine-catalogs/epc/toyota-general/corolla/AE86L|title=Spare parts for Toyota Corolla, AE86L (GEN)|website=www.amayama.com}}</ref>

In Australia, the AE86 was also based on the general specification Corolla SR, but marketed as the Toyota Sprinter liftback. It featured the taillights from the Trueno but only came with the 4A-C engine.<ref name=AUAE86>{{cite web|url=http://www.aeu86.org/ae86-brochures/australian-ae86-brochure-toyota-sprinter-1983-10/|title=Australian Toyota Sprinter AE86 brochure 1983-10|access-date=2020-11-26}}</ref>

The AE86 Corolla GT liftback was sold in the Middle East ([[Gulf Cooperation Council|GCC]]) with the exterior of the North American market Corolla GT-S, but lacked the rear [[Automotive lighting#Side marker lights and reflectors|side marker lights]] and featured a three-spoke steering wheel. It only came with the general specification 4A-GE engine and five-speed manual gearbox with an optional LSD.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amayama.com/en/genuine-catalogs/epc/toyota-general/corolla/AE86L/856|title=Spare parts for Toyota Corolla, AE86L-ECMQFV|website=www.amayama.com}}</ref>

== H2 and BEV concepts ==
In January 2023 at the [[Tokyo Auto Salon]], [[Toyota Gazoo Racing]] (TGR) and [[Lexus]] exhibited two AE86 liftbacks concept cars called H2 and BEV Concepts that have been converted to run using a hydrogen engine and a battery-electric system. The H2 concept was based on the Sprinter Trueno and converted by TGR to run on [[Hydrogen internal combustion engine vehicle|hydrogen fuel]] while retaining the original 1.6 L engine that received special modifications, including fuel injectors, fuel pipes, and spark plugs and combined with two high-pressure [[Hydrogen infrastructure#Hydrogen tank|hydrogen storage tanks]] from the [[Toyota Mirai#JPD20|Mirai]]. The BEV concept was based on the Corolla Levin that was converted as a [[battery electric vehicle]] by Lexus by combining an electric motor from [[Toyota Tundra#XK70|Thundra Hybrid]], an 18.1-kWh battery from [[Toyota Prius Plug-in Hybrid#XW60|Prius PHEV]]/[[Lexus RX#ALA10|Lexus RX450h+]] and also featured a manual transmission.<ref>{{cite press release|url=https://global.toyota/en/newsroom/corporate/38537253.html|title=Exhibiting at Tokyo Auto Salon 2023 and Tokyo Outdoor Show|date=13 January 2023|publisher=Toyota}}</ref>

==Motorsports==
{{more citations needed|date=July 2018}}
During its production run, the AE86 was a popular choice for showroom stock, [[Group A]], and [[Group N]] racing, especially in [[rallying]] and circuit races. It competed in the under 2.0 L class, mostly in 1401 to 1600 cc A6 or N2 classes. After the production ended, many privateer teams continued to race the AE86, and it remains a popular choice for rallying and club races today.

Part of the continued appeal of the AE86 for motorsports is its rear-drive configuration, not available in most newer lightweight coupes. In Group A [[touring car racing|touring car races]], the car either dominated the lower category where eligible or fought it out with [[Honda Civic]]s or the later [[Toyota Corolla (E90)|AE92s]] and [[Toyota Corolla (E100)|AE101s]] whilst maintaining its competitiveness. In Ireland, where rallying is considered one of the most popular forms of motorsport, as organizing regulations are more relaxed compared to that of other countries, the AE86 was popular when new, and remains so popular that teams will purchase cars from the UK and Japan due to local shortages. The AE86 is also popular for rally use in Finland, where the cars can be competitive in the F-Cup competition for naturally aspirated 2WD cars.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ewrc-results.com/entries/14776-rakennusliike-khamalainen-rantaralli-2013/?sct=236|title=37. Rakennusliike K.Hämäläinen Rantaralli 2013|website=www.ewrc-results.com}}</ref>

From 1984 until late 1990s, many privateer teams competed with AE86s in [[World Rally Championship]] (WRC) events. Some of them found success by winning their class and sometimes became eligible to score WRC championship points when they finished in the top ten of the overall classifications. The first respectable result was in the [[1984 World Rally Championship|1984]] [[Rally de Portugal]], when driver Jorge Ortigão and co-driver João Baptista finished in second place behind the Group A class winner, the [[Volkswagen Golf Mk1|Volkswagen Golf GTi (Mk1)]], and finished in eighth place overall among the more powerful [[Group B]] cars.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ewrc-results.com/final/5493-rallye-de-portugal-vinho-do-porto-1984/?sct=1|title=18. Rallye de Portugal - Vinho do Porto 1984|website=www.ewrc-results.com}}</ref> The first class win came three rounds later in the [[Acropolis Rally]], when Manolis Halivelakis and Konstantinos Exarchos finished thirteenth overall.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ewrc-results.com/final/8559-rothmans-acropolis-rally-1984/?sct=1|title=31. Rothmans Acropolis Rally 1984|website=www.ewrc-results.com}}</ref> The best result of AE86 in WRC was in the [[1989 World Rally Championship|1989]] [[Rallye Côte d'Ivoire]] when Adolphe Choteau and Jean-Pierre Claverie finished third overall.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ewrc-results.com/final/8626-rallye-cote-divoire-1989/?sct=1|title=21. Rallye Côte d'Ivoire 1989|website=www.ewrc-results.com}}</ref>

The AE86 competed in the Division 1 [[European Touring Car Championship]] (ETCC) from 1984 to 1988, where its main rivals were the [[Volkswagen Golf Mk2|Volkswagen Golf GTi (Mk2)]] and [[Audi 80#B2|Audi 80 GLE]]. In 1986 it beat the Division  2 [[BMW 3 Series (E30)|BMW 325i (E30)]] and Division 3 [[BMW 6 Series (E24)|BMW 635i CSi]] to win the Manufacturers Championship with 267 points.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.touringcarracing.net/Pages/1986%20Class.html |title=European Touring Car championship - 1986 |website=www.touringcarracing.net}}</ref>

In 1986 and 1987, [[Chris Hodgetts]] won the British Touring Car Championship ([[BTCC]]), beating the V8 [[Rover SD1]]'s, [[Ford Sierra]] Cosworth's and [[BMW 3 Series (E30)]] M3's two years running for an overall points victory driving an AE86 for [[Toyota (GB) PLC]] and his own race prep team CHMS.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.btcc.net/history/champions/btcc-champions/ |title=BTCC Champions |website=British Touring Car Championship |access-date=2021-05-04}}</ref>

Five different teams won eight of eleven races in Division 1 class in the [[1987 World Touring Car Championship]] (WTCC). However, none of these teams were eligible to score championship points.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.racingsportscars.com/championship/WTCC.html|title=Season: 1987 (World Touring Car Championship)|website=www.racingsportscars.com}}</ref> The Corolla GT also successfully dominated its class in European endurance races like the [[Spa 24 Hours]] and [[Nürburgring 24 Hours]] throughout the 1980s.

From 1985 to 1988, the Corolla Levin participated in Division 1 of the [[All Japan Touring Car Championship]] (JTC). [[Kaoru Hoshino]], from the Trampio Levin team, won the 1985 Division 1 class championship and placed third overall with two wins and two second-place finishes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://motorsports.jaf.or.jp/results/search?competitions=01RC001&sort=far&from=1985-01&to=1985-12&championship=06ZZ001&series=09RC010|title=国内競技結果（リザルト）検索 (1985)|language=Japanese|website=motorsports.jaf.or.jp}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://touringcarracing.net/Pages/1985%20AJTCC%20Class.html|title=1985 All-Japan Touring Car Championship
|website=touringcarracing.net}}</ref> In the following seasons, the AE86 faced a fierce battle from the [[Honda Civic (third generation)|Civic Si]] and was also overshadowed by the more competitive front-wheel drive [[Toyota Corolla (E80)|AE82 Corolla FX-GT]]. The semi-factory supported Kraft team entered a spaceframe Trueno in the [[All Japan Grand Touring Car Championship|JGTC]] for the [[Super GT#GT300|GT300]] regulations in 1999. The Trueno used a [[Dallara]] [[Formula Three|F3]] chassis and was powered with a [[Toyota S engine#3S-GTE|3S-GTE]] engine that came from a [[Toyota MR2 (W20)|SW20 MR2 Turbo]] that produces about {{Convert|300|hp|kW|0|abbr=on}}. Despite being popular with the fans, the car had minor success and was abandoned from use halfway through the 2001 season when the AE86 burst into flames during the third round of the season at [[Sportsland SUGO|Sugo]]. Kraft subsequently replaced it with the newly-delivered [[Toyota MR-S]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.whichcar.com.au/features/weirdest-race-cars-of-jgtc|title=The weirdest cars to race in Japan's JGTC/SuperGT championship|date=6 January 2022|work=WhichCar|author=Alex Affat|access-date=5 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.as-web.jp/racing-on/697310?all|title=【忘れがたき銘車たち】懐かしい"ハチロク"が最新鋭マシンに⁉︎『JGTC AE86型スプリンタートレノ』|date=17 May 2021|work=auto sport Web|language=ja|trans-title=[Unforgettable famous cars] Nostalgic "Hachiroku" turned into a state-of-the-art machine!? ︎ "JGTC AE86 Sprinter Trueno"|access-date=5 October 2022}}</ref>

The [[Toyota Team Australia]] (TAA)-prepared AE86s dominated the under 2.0 L class in the [[Australian Touring Car Championship]], the [[Australian Endurance Championship]], and the [[Australian 2.0 Litre Touring Car Championship]] from 1985 to 1986.<ref name=Shannons>{{cite web|url=https://club.shannons.com.au/club/news/racing-garage/toyota-corolla-ae86-sprinter-a-runaway-winner/|title=Toyota Corolla AE86 Sprinter: A Runaway Winner!|date=9 November 2017|website=club.shannons.com.au}}</ref> TTA secured five class titles across those championships: four by [[John Smith (racing driver, born 1952)|John Smith]] and one by Mike Quinn in the [[1986 Australian Endurance Championship]]. The AE86 was also highly successful at the [[Bathurst 1000]], although its victories were mostly against other AE86s and the front-wheel drive AE82. The TTA AE86s secured class victories in [[1985 James Hardie 1000|1985]], [[1986 James Hardie 1000|1986]] and [[1988 Tooheys 1000|1988]].<ref name=Shannons/> Following their success, privateer teams running the local market Sprinter liftback model also achieved victories: [[Bob Holden (racing driver)|Bob Holden Motors]] won in [[1987 James Hardie 1000|1987]], Phoenix Motorsport in [[1990 Tooheys 1000|1990]], and Speedtech Motorsport in [[1991 Tooheys 1000|1991]].

The rear wheel drive configuration, combined with the AE86's light weight (approximately 2300 lb (950–970 kg) curb weight), balance and relatively powerful (and easy to tune) [[Toyota 4A-GE|4A-GEU]] engine made it popular among the Japanese ''[[hashiriya]]'' (street racers in Japanese), many of whom raced in ''[[Street racing#Japan|touge]]'' (mountain passes in Japanese) where the corners suited the AE86 best, especially on the downhill.<ref name=driftjapan /> Among those who utilized this car was Japanese racing legend [[Keiichi Tsuchiya]] also known as the ''Drift King'' ("Dori-Kin" in Japanese). Tsuchiya who also drove the AE86 Levin in the JTC,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://motorsports.jaf.or.jp/results/search/1985/race/1985-9999-97|title=国際ツーリングカー耐久レース インターTEC グループA　(1) リザルト|language=Japanese|website=motorsports.jaf.or.jp}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://global.toyota/en/corolla50th/story/04/|title=A Corolla, But Not An Economy Car - Why I Still Drive My AE86|date=8 November 2016|publisher=Toyota}}</ref> helped popularize the sport of [[drifting (motorsport)|drifting]], which involves taking a car on a set of controlled slides through corners.<ref name=driftjapan /> The AE86's FR configuration made it well suited to this kind of cornering, and currently the car is a mainstay of drift shows and competitions. Japanese drifters like [[Katsuhiro Ueo]] (champion of [[2002 D1 Grand Prix series]] with AE86), [[Toshiki Yoshioka]], [[Youichi Imamura]], [[Kouichi Yamashita]], Hiroshi Takahashi, [[Tetsuya Hibino]], and Wataru Hayashi were also involved in making the AE86 famous in the drift scene. AE86s around the world have been extensively modified for use in professional drifting.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://jalopnik.com/europeans-have-to-out-crazy-japan-when-it-comes-to-drif-1659605889 |title=Europeans Have To Out-Crazy Japan When It Comes To Drift Cars |first=Máté |last=Petrány |work=Jalopnik |date=2014-11-21 |access-date=2018-02-01}}</ref> The AE86 is also a popular choice for [[autocross]], [[Gymkhana (motorsport)|gymkhana]], [[Time trial #Motorsport|time attack]], [[rallycross]], and [[hillclimbing]] events.

==In popular culture==
[[File:Toyota SPRINTER TRUENO GT-APEX (E-AE86-FCMVF) ver.INITIAL D.jpg|thumb|''Initial D'' AE86 replica]]

The AE86 is considered as an iconic [[cultural icon]] in [[Japanese popular culture]] following its inclusion in the ''[[Initial D]]'' anime and manga. The main character, Takumi Fujiwara, uses his father's AE86 Trueno GT APEX liftback to make his [[tofu]] deliveries and later for racing. His friend, Itsuki Takeuchi, drives an AE85 Levin SR liftback. Throughout the series, two of Takumi's opponents drive AE86s: Wataru Akiyama, who drives a turbocharged (later supercharged) AE86 Levin GT APEX liftback, and Shinji Inui, who drives the notchback coupé version of the GT APEX AE86 Trueno. The AE86 is also a playable vehicle in the ''[[Initial D Arcade Stage]]'' series. The popularity of ''Initial D'' is cited as the main cause of the car's high resale price, which is often referred to as "Takumi tax" or "tofu tax", after Takumi and his tofu delivery occupation respectively.<ref>{{cite web |last=O'Mara |first=Sean |date=2013-01-28 |title=The Enduring Legacy of ''Initial D'' and the AE86 |url=http://otakuusamagazine.com/Anime/News1/The_Enduring_Legacy_of_Initial_D_and_the_AE86_4941.aspx |access-date=2013-02-01}}</ref>

==Production==
The Toyota AE86 (as well as the AE85) was built in either the Kanto Higashi-Fuji plant, or the [[Takaoka plant]]. Over 360,000 AE86s are estimated to have been built in total.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://jalopnik.com/toyota-made-10x-as-many-ae86s-as-you-think-1841642582|title=Toyota Made 10x As Many AE86s As You Think|author=Orlove, R.|publisher=Jalopnik|date=12 February 2020}}</ref>

AE86s built at the (now-closed)<ref name=higashiclosure/> Kanto Higashi-Fuji plant came with a "5" designation at the beginning of the serial number. Their plant codes were "M21" and "M22". Only 28% of AE86s were produced at this plant, all of them being made for Japan with no export models being made.

AE86s built at the Takaoka plant came with a "0" designation at the beginning of the serial number. Their plant codes were "A54" and "A52". The majority of AE86s were produced at this plant (including exported AE86 models), as it was the original plant where the Toyota Corolla and Sprinter are manufactured.

extract:
The AE86 series of the Toyota Corolla Levin/Sprinter Trueno are small, front-engine/rear-wheel-drive compact cars within the mostly front-engine/front-wheel-drive fifth generation Corolla (E80) range—marketed and manufactured by Toyota from 1983 to 1987 in coupé and liftback configurations. It was the last production Corolla to feature rear-wheel drive.
The cars were light, affordable, easily modifiable, and had a five-speed manual transmission, a limited-slip differential (optional), MacPherson strut front suspension, near 50/50 front/rear weight balance, and a front-engine/rear-drive layout—at a time when this configuration was waning industry-wide.  In certain areas of the world (and optional in others) it was powered by a high revving (7800 rpm) twin-cam engine.  
Widely popular for Showroom Stock, Group A, and Group N, Rally and Club racing, the cars' inherent qualities also earned the AE86 an early and enduring international prominence in the motorsport discipline of drifting. The AE86 was featured centrally in the popular, long-running Japanese manga and anime series titled Initial D (1995–2013) as the main character's drift and tofu delivery car. In 2015, Road & Track called the AE86 "a cult icon, inextricably interwoven with the earliest days of drifting."
The AE86 would go on to inspire the Toyota 86 (2012–present), a 2+2 sports car jointly developed by Toyota and Subaru, manufactured by Subaru—and marketed also as the Toyota GT86, Toyota GR86, Toyota FT86, Scion FR-S and Subaru BRZ.
In November 2021, Toyota temporarily restarted the production of a limited number of parts for the AE86, with dealers beginning to take orders for new steering knuckle arms and rear brake calipers. Rear axle half shafts have also been scheduled for new production. Toyota has also announced that this reboot is temporary, and parts will only be available as long as stocks last.
